goal.why: I want my technical memos to sound clear and confident to my director.

sessions.title: Impact: zero-downtime database migration
sessions.prompt: Write the "Impact" section of a promotion document for a senior engineer who led a database migration with zero downtime.
sessions.text: Maria led the migration of our main Postgres cluster from version 11 to 16. She designed a dual-write plan, wrote the runbook, and coordinated four teams. We finished the migration in six weeks with zero downtime and no data loss.

iterations.text: Maria led the migration of our main Postgres cluster from version 11 to 16. She designed a dual-write plan, wrote the runbook, and coordinated four teams. We finished the migration in six weeks with zero downtime and no data loss.

review.summary: Clear and concrete. Add the business impact: what the migration made possible.
improvements: Say why the migration mattered to the business.

sessions.title: The night before the launch
sessions.prompt: Write a short story (200–400 words) about the night before a big product launch. Show the feeling; do not name it.
sessions.text:
The night before the launch, I stayed in the office until midnight. The floor was empty and quiet. I was very nervous. I could hear the air conditioner hum above my desk.

Maria came back with two coffees. "We are not ready." she said quietly. She put a cup next to my keyboard. I felt tired and afraid.

We read the release notes again. We checked the dashboards again. We ran the smoke tests again. We fixed one small bug again.

At two o'clock, after six hours of failed runs and cold coffee, the build is finally green. She looks at me and smiles. Then she laughed, stood up, and turned off the lights.

iterations.text:
The night before the launch, I stayed in the office until midnight. The floor was empty and quiet. I was very nervous. I could hear the air conditioner hum above my desk.

Maria came back with two coffees. "We are not ready." she said quietly. She put a cup next to my keyboard. I felt tired and afraid.

We read the release notes again. We checked the dashboards again. We ran the smoke tests again. We fixed one small bug again.

At two o'clock, after six hours of failed runs and cold coffee, the build is finally green. She looks at me and smiles. Then she laughed, stood up, and turned off the lights.

review.summary: A clear scene with a real turning point. The writing names feelings instead of showing them, and the last paragraph moves from the past tense to the present.
strengths: Concrete details: two coffees, the air conditioner, cold coffee.
The repeated "again" paragraph shows the long night well.
improvements: Show the fear and the tiredness through actions, not with "nervous" and "afraid".
Keep the past tense in the last paragraph.
Use a comma before the dialogue tag.

corrections.explanation: Use a comma, not a period, before a dialogue tag.
The story is in the past tense. Keep it in the past.

corrections.original: She looks at me and smiles.
corrections.suggestion: She looked at me and smiled.
corrections.explanation: Keep the past tense in the narration.

corrections.suggestion: My hands would not stay still on the keyboard.
corrections.explanation: Show the feeling through an action instead of naming it.

corrections.original: I could hear the air conditioner hum
corrections.explanation: Remove the filter "I could hear" and show the sound directly.

patterns: Naming emotions instead of showing them
review.rewrite:
The night before the launch, I stayed in the office until midnight. The floor was empty and quiet. My hands would not stay still on the keyboard, and the air conditioner hummed above my desk.

Maria came back with two coffees. "We are not ready," she said, and set a cup next to my keyboard. I rubbed my eyes and did not answer.

We read the release notes again. We checked the dashboards. We ran the smoke tests one more time, and then we fixed one small bug.

At two o'clock, after six hours of failed runs and cold coffee, the build was finally green. She looked at me and smiled. Then she laughed, stood up, and turned off the lights.
review.next_exercise: Rewrite the sentence "I felt tired and afraid." without emotion words. Use one action, one thing that Maria says, and one detail of the room.

criteria.name: Arc
criteria.comment: A clear setup and a turning point at two o'clock. The ending comes a little fast.

criteria.name: Show, don't tell
criteria.comment: You name the feelings: nervous, tired, afraid. Show them through actions and details.

criteria.name: Specific detail
criteria.comment: Good details: two coffees, the air conditioner. Add one sensory detail per paragraph.

criteria.name: Rhythm
criteria.comment: The "again" paragraph works once, but many sentences have the same short shape.

criteria.name: Consistency
criteria.comment: The last paragraph moves from the past tense to the present.

criteria.name: Dialogue
criteria.comment: The line sounds natural, but use a comma before "she said".

sessions.title: Ship the export without load tests?
sessions.prompt: A product manager asks: "Can we ship the export feature on Friday if we skip the load tests?"
sessions.text:
Hi Priya,

Great question! To give you some context, the export feature reads all rows of a report at once, and last month a large customer exported 2 million rows and the service ran out of memory, which is why we added the load tests in the first place. The tests takes two days. We could skip them. But it is risky. If we skip them, the first big export can crash the service for everyone.

My suggestion is that we ship on Friday behind a feature flag, turn it on for small customers first, watch the memory graphs over the weekend, and run the load tests on Monday before we turn it on for everyone.

Does that work for you?

iterations.text:
Hi Priya,

Great question! To give you some context, the export feature reads all rows of a report at once, and last month a large customer exported 2 million rows and the service ran out of memory, which is why we added the load tests in the first place. The tests takes two days. We could skip them. But it is risky. If we skip them, the first big export can crash the service for everyone.

My suggestion is that we ship on Friday behind a feature flag, turn it on for small customers first, watch the memory graphs over the weekend, and run the load tests on Monday before we turn it on for everyone.

Does that work for you?

review.summary: The content is right, but the answer is hidden. Priya must read about 100 words to learn that the answer is "no, but here is a safe plan".
strengths: You explain the real risk with a concrete example: 2 million rows.
You end with a clear question for the reader.
improvements: Put the answer in the first sentence: "No, not safely, but we can ship behind a flag."
Split the second paragraph, and write the plan as a short list.

corrections.original: Great question! To give you some context, the export feature
corrections.suggestion: No, not safely. The export feature
corrections.explanation: Answer the question in the first sentence. Give the context after it.

corrections.original: which is why we added the load tests in the first place
corrections.suggestion: so we added the load tests
corrections.explanation: Say the same thing with fewer words.

corrections.original: We could skip them. But it is risky.
corrections.suggestion: We could skip them, but it is risky.
corrections.explanation: Join two short sentences that make one point.

corrections.original: My suggestion is that we ship
corrections.explanation: Use the verb "suggest", not the noun "suggestion". It is shorter and more direct.

review.rewrite:
Hi Priya,

No, not safely. But we can still ship on Friday with a safer plan:

- Ship behind a feature flag.
- Turn it on for small customers first.
- Watch the memory graphs over the weekend.
- Run the load tests on Monday, then turn it on for everyone.

Why: last month, a 2-million-row export made the service run out of memory. The load tests catch this, but they take two days.

Does that work for you?
review.next_exercise: Take a long reply that you sent this week. Rewrite its first sentence so that it answers the question in 12 words or less. Move the context below it.

criteria.name: Answer first
criteria.comment: The answer comes in the third paragraph.

criteria.name: Easy to scan
criteria.comment: One long paragraph, and the plan is a list inside one sentence.

criteria.name: Plain language
criteria.comment: Mostly simple words, but two sentences are too long.

criteria.name: Complete
criteria.comment: It gives the risk, a plan, and a next step.

criteria.name: Concise
criteria.comment: About 40% of the words can go.

sessions.title: Move billing from polling to webhooks
sessions.prompt: Write a technical memo that explains why your team will move from REST polling to webhooks. Start with the decision, then the context, then the risks.
sessions.text:
Decision: we will move the billing service from REST polling to webhooks in Q1.

Context: Today our system polls the payment provider every 30 seconds. It creates a lot of unnecessary load and in order to reduce the costs we need to change the approach. The polling was implemented by previous team three years ago, and since that time the traffic is grown five times. In the last month we had two incidents, when the provider was rate limiting us and the invoices were not updated during 2 hours, which was very painful for the customers and for the support team that had to answer on many tickets.

Risks: I think the main risk is that webhooks can be lost. We will utilize a retry queue and a daily reconciliation job to protect against this.

iterations.text: We will move billing to webhooks. Currently our system is polling the provider every 30 seconds and it creates a lot of load. The polling was implemented by previous team and since that time the traffic is grown five times.

review.summary: The decision is clear, but the context is thin and there are several grammar errors.
patterns: Present perfect for changes over time

review.summary: Good structure. The context paragraph has one very long sentence and a few grammar slips.

corrections.explanation: Use "the" before a specific team that the reader knows.
Use "for" with a length of time.

iterations.text:
Decision: we will move the billing service from REST polling to webhooks in Q1.

Context: Today our system polls the payment provider every 30 seconds. It creates a lot of unnecessary load and in order to reduce the costs we need to change the approach. The polling was implemented by previous team three years ago, and since that time the traffic is grown five times. In the last month we had two incidents, when the provider was rate limiting us and the invoices were not updated during 2 hours, which was very painful for the customers and for the support team that had to answer on many tickets.

Risks: I think the main risk is that webhooks can be lost. We will utilize a retry queue and a daily reconciliation job to protect against this.

review.summary: Much better than the first draft: the memo now has a clear decision, evidence, and risks. The remaining problems are articles, two prepositions, one tense error, and a 50-word sentence in the context.
strengths: Bottom line up front: the first line gives the decision.
The incidents are concrete evidence for the change.
improvements: Split the incident sentence into two or three sentences.
Remove hedges such as "I think" in the Risks section. State the risk directly.

corrections.explanation: Use "the" before a noun that the reader already knows.
Use the present perfect for a change from the past until now.
Use "for" with a length of time; "during" goes with a named period.
"Answer" takes a direct object, with no preposition.
Do not put a comma before a clause that defines the noun.

corrections.original: It creates a lot of unnecessary load and in order to reduce the costs we need to change the approach.
corrections.suggestion: This creates unnecessary load. To cut costs, we need a different approach.
corrections.explanation: Two short sentences are easier to read than one long one.

patterns: Present perfect for changes over time
